clinicalPearls: Painless hematuria, either gross or microscopic, is the initial manifestation of urinary tract cancer in most patients; in males painless hematuria is almost always abnormal and must be worked up (Harrison 22e p.691).

In females, hematuria due to malignancy is often mistaken for a urinary tract infection or menstrual bleeding; antibiotics are warranted if a concurrent UTI is found, but persistent hematuria still requires further workup (Harrison 22e p.691).

Initial investigation in either sex includes urine cytology plus visual examination of the bladder by cystoscopy, together with radiographic evaluation of the kidneys and upper tract by CT urogram (MR urogram if renal function is poor) (Harrison 22e p.691).

Smoking of tobacco products is the overwhelming leading risk factor; 90% of new bladder cancer diagnoses occur in current or former smokers, and roughly one-third of cases could be prevented by smoking cessation (Harrison 22e p.692).

Urothelial carcinoma (formerly transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common histology, seen in about 90% of cases; nonurothelial variants (squamous cell, adenocarcinoma, small-cell, carcinosarcoma) collectively account for 10% or less (Harrison 22e p.690-691).

Disease is divided into non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC: carcinoma in situ, Ta, or T1 not reaching the muscularis propria; ~75% at presentation) and muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC: T2 invasion of muscularis propria and beyond) (Harrison 22e p.691-692).

Urothelial carcinoma shows a biphasic phenotype: low-grade papillary tumors that frequently recur but rarely invade or metastasize, and high-grade often flat tumors that invade early and lead to lethal metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.691).
harrison.pathophysiology: Urothelial carcinoma arises from the lining of the bladder, renal pelvis, ureter, and urethra and displays a biphasic clinical behavior. Loss of portions of chromosomes 9q and 9p (loss of heterozygosity) is an early molecular event in both phenotypes; candidate genes in these regions include CDKN2A and TSC1. Low-grade papillary tumors are characterized by RAS/RAF pathway alterations with activating FGFR3 mutations or fusions in 60-80% of patients, whereas the high-grade invasive phenotype features early deleterious TP53 and RB1 mutations, CDH1 (E-cadherin) alterations, and increased VEGFR2 expression. Chronic inflammatory states drive squamous-type bladder cancer, classically chronic schistosomiasis infection and chronic indwelling catheters in paraplegic patients. Carcinogenic exposures include aromatic amines (benzidine, beta-naphthylamine) in industrial dyes and arsenic-contaminated drinking water. The Cancer Genome Atlas defined five intrinsic molecular subtypes (luminal papillary, luminal infiltrated, luminal, basal squamous, neuronal) resembling breast cancer subclasses (Harrison 22e p.691-692).
infectionMimics: Hematuria from malignancy in females is frequently mistaken for a urinary tract infection (Harrison 22e p.691).
nonInfectiousMimics: In females, malignant hematuria may be misattributed to menstrual bleeding (Harrison 22e p.691).

Intravesical BCG side effects (dysuria, urinary frequency, bladder spasms, hematuria) overlap with infection/cystitis, and in <5% a systemic inflammatory response can mimic disseminated BCG infection (Harrison 22e p.692).
additionalInvestigations: Urine cytology (detects cancer in only about 50% of high-grade bladder cancers) (Harrison 22e p.691).

Cystoscopy for direct bladder visualization; blue light or narrow-band imaging cystoscopy improves detection of small or flat noninvasive tumors and is used routinely in monitoring (Harrison 22e p.691).
CT urogram (or MR urogram if renal function is impaired) for the kidneys and upper tract (Harrison 22e p.691).

Adjunct urine molecular tests (FISH for chromosomal changes, nuclear mitotic proteins, bladder tumor-associated antigens) used mainly for detecting recurrence, as they can be falsely positive (Harrison 22e p.691).
Ureteroscopy or retrograde pyelography when upper-tract tumors are suspected with a normal bladder (Harrison 22e p.691).
Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) or endoscopic resection of upper tract tumors for histologic diagnosis and staging (Harrison 22e p.691).
Genomic sequencing of tumor tissue and/or circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) recommended in all metastatic patients (Harrison 22e p.690).
redFlags: Painless gross or microscopic hematuria warrants investigation for urothelial cancer; in males it is almost always abnormal (Harrison 22e p.691).
Persistent hematuria despite treatment of a concurrent UTI requires further workup (Harrison 22e p.691).
Flank pain with an upper tract renal pelvis/ureter cancer, or hydronephrosis from a bladder tumor obstructing the ureteral orifice (Harrison 22e p.691).
Cachexia and widespread metastatic disease at presentation (rare) (Harrison 22e p.691).
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes correlate closely with stage at diagnosis. About 75% present with non-muscle-invasive disease, 18% with muscle-invasive disease, and only 3% with metastatic spread. 5-year overall survival is 70-90% for disease confined to the bladder (stage I-II), 39-50% for disease penetrating through the bladder or involving regional lymph nodes (stage III), and only 8% for metastatic disease (stage IV) (Harrison 22e p.692).
pitfalls: Urine cytology is insensitive, identifying cancer in only about 50% of high-grade bladder cancers, so a negative cytology does not exclude malignancy (Harrison 22e p.691).
Treating presumed UTI without follow-up risks missing malignancy; persistent hematuria after antibiotics still requires workup (Harrison 22e p.691).
Adjunct urine molecular tests may be abnormal in patients without cancer (false positives) and are best reserved for surveillance of known cancer (Harrison 22e p.691).
Systemic inflammatory reaction after intravesical BCG can mimic disseminated BCG infection (Harrison 22e p.692).
harrison.severityClassification: Staging is driven primarily by depth of invasion (T stage). NMIBC: Tis (CIS) and Ta (epithelial layer only) or T1 (into connective tissue/lamina propria below urothelium but not muscularis propria). MIBC: T2 (into muscularis propria), T3 (through muscularis propria to serosa), T4 (adjacent pelvic organs - rectum, prostate, vagina, cervix). Nodal: N1 (single true pelvic node), N2 (two true pelvic nodes), N3 (common iliac nodes); disease beyond common iliac nodes or distant spread is M1. Stages 0a-II are defined by T stage alone without nodal/metastatic disease; regional pelvic or common iliac nodal involvement is stage III; any distant metastasis is stage IV (Harrison 22e p.691-692).
management: For non-muscle-invasive disease, transurethral resection of bladder tumour followed by intravesical BCG immunotherapy or intravesical chemotherapy to reduce recurrence and progression
For muscle-invasive disease, neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy with radical cystectomy, or bladder-preserving chemoradiotherapy in selected patients
For advanced or metastatic disease, platinum-based chemotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted options such as FGFR inhibitors or antibody-drug conjugates
Smoking cessation as the key modifiable risk factor influencing recurrence and new tumour formation
Surveillance cystoscopy with urine cytology to detect recurrence, using blue-light or narrow-band imaging for subtle flat lesions
Evaluate the upper tracts with CT urography and treat upper-tract urothelial tumours accordingly
Coordinate care through a urology and oncology multidisciplinary team
